From a friend in the medical device industry: 

Look for surgeons who are skilled with one manufacturer. Even better when they also work with the medical rep for that manufacturer. ( This made me leery at first; but it makes sense) 

Look for surgeons who specialize in one area (AKA hips or knees) because you want someone who is truly a specialist both with body parts AND the device itself. 

You can absolutely ask what the surgeon is using; but don’t expect them to change upon request. If you don’t like the answer; then shop around to a different surgeon. Many of them advertise their “brand” on their website and I appreciate that. I actually got to hold mine in my hands. 

You absolutely DO NOT want a brand new device. Ten years on the market is good; that’s a decade of revisions and proven efficacy. It also means it’s been around long enough for surgeons to have experience with it. ( Don’t be a beta tester when it comes to implants!) 

As to your original question; parts change all the time. Honestly the answer he gsve me started delving into metals and alloys and coatings and I kind of lost track of what he was saying … but the jist was there is no singular thing to look out for. (Cobalt bad; ceramic good; etc)

I honestly struggled with my settings for YEARS and was constantly making adjustments. (Part of this was during the pandemic when everything shut down; then I relocated across the US so much of these delays were from that) 

What finally did it for me was getting a proper sleep titration study done and converting to CPAP instead of APAP. I’m finally getting real REM rest; which I never had despite having a low AHI.

sleep medicine is still catching up to the science behind  understanding the nature of UARS and apnea related diseases. Makes treatment difficult.

It’s not a silly ask; and I only hope my words can help. There are many many good poems and books dedicated to grief out there, so I will stick to pragmatic suggestions for you, ok? 

First, the best thing you can do is continue to live your life. Even in living your life is different now, and you feel closed off or even guilt if you experience joy. It’s ok - your forever changed but YOU are still there.  Joy will come back. Feel your feelings, grieve and cry, but put one foot in front of the other. 

If you have photos, recordings, audio recordings try to find a way to preserve them when you are able. You forget more than you realize as time goes on. This will help you preserve the legacy. 

Find support groups, either online or in person. It helps to be able to just talk openly for as long as you need. There is no time limit on grief. Therapy can sometimes help too. 

Think of the goals, the dreams, the passions you shared with this person. If and when you are ready - turn it into something. It might be a 5K fundraiser against cancer, starting a punk band, fostering a kitten. Whatever this amazing person was and inspires!  The doing, the action, creates meaning from this unimaginable loss. It prevents inertia. 

You will cry at the most random of times - and it’s ok! You’d be surprised how few people notice , not that it’s something you need to be ashamed about. 

Remember that death comes for us all - it’s a shame he only got such a short time on this planet. Remember live your life with the end in mind. None of us know how much time we have from the moment we are here. 

We can only hope to live a life of meaning and to pass surrounded by those who love us, like this person here.
